issues: Adding p ≠ q narrows the universal quantifier, so it strengthens the negated claim rather than weakening it. B (there exist distinct p, q with no suitable n) implies the negation of A as written. It is also the only non-degenerate reading of A: for p = q the property fails trivially, since p cannot divide both n and n+1. So the hypothesis removes a triviality and does not tailor the statement to the route. The witness p=2, q=7 is distinct, matching the notes' resolution.

Restricting to n ≥ 2 weakens the 'no n exists' conclusion only nominally. P(1) is undefined, and with the divisibility encoding neither n = 0 nor n = 1 can satisfy both conditions (n = 0 fails the 'every prime dividing n is ≤ p' clause), so nothing is lost.
The divisibility encoding (p | n and every prime divisor of n is ≤ p) correctly captures P(n) = p for n ≥ 2.

faithful.backtranslation:
For an integer n ≥ 2, write P(n) for the largest prime factor of n. The theorem claims the following: it is **not** true that for every pair of distinct primes p and q there is a natural number n ≥ 2 with P(n) = p and P(n+1) = q.

Equivalently, there exist two distinct primes p ≠ q for which no natural number n ≥ 2 has both of these properties:
- p divides n and every prime dividing n is at most p;
- q divides n+1 and every prime dividing n+1 is at most q.
